title: Equity & Access Wraparound Services
author: Jared
summary: Jared, a seventh grade ELA teacher at a Baltimore community school, translates the jargon of wraparound services for teachers and families. He defines the term as a school that helps students and their families with the barriers that make learning hard, and he insists that what separates real wraparound from a list of programs is a coordinator who connects each student to a provider and services that are actually accessible. He explains why middle school is the hard test, since needs grow just as adult visibility shrinks across six or seven teachers. He then weighs the evidence honestly: RAND found lower chronic absenteeism and fewer discipline incidents in New York City community schools, while an MDRC trial of Communities In Schools found better relationships but no change in grades or attendance after two years. His conclusion is that wraparound is not a fast test-score strategy but clears the path to learning. The piece closes with concrete guidance for teachers, parents and local partners.
points: The difference between real wraparound services and a list of programs is coordination and access, so the useful question in any meeting is who coordinates it and how a kid actually gets connected.
The teacher's role is to notice and refer on patterns rather than diagnose, which means knowing the coordinator by name and exactly how referrals work in your building.
The evidence is uneven: attendance and discipline improve reliably in NYC community schools, while reading scores and, in some trials, grades and behavior did not move.
Middle schoolers hide need behind complaints about boredom, so adult visibility drops just as problems grow, which is why this age group is the real test.
Quality matters more than quantity, since NYC schools with stronger mental health supports cut absenteeism the most.
quotes: Veteran teacher me considers something else: she skipped breakfast, or she was up at 5 getting her little brother to daycare, or a tooth has hurt for two weeks and nobody has had time to get her to a dentist.
Coordination. Someone, usually a community school coordinator, knows the student, knows the providers, and connects the two. Without that person, services exist on paper and nobody uses them.
A second grader will tell you her stomach hurts. A seventh grader will tell you the book is boring.
The teacher’s job isn’t to solve any of that. It’s to notice and refer. The coordinator’s job is to make sure the referral goes somewhere.
Attendance is the strongest result. RAND studied New York City’s community schools from 2015–16 through 2017–18.
My read: wraparound services aren’t a fast test-score strategy. They clear the path, though. Quality matters, too.

A kid who is hungry, hurting, or unsure where she’s sleeping tonight is not available to learn about theme. Wraparound services don’t replace good teaching. They make it possible for students to show up for it.
